children.author: pavon
children.text: Training in-house has never been a skill issue, it is a budget issue of collecting and labeling enough training data.

¿Por qué no los dos? Big skill issue, you can even route known problems to a trained in-house simple classifier and low-confidence problems to Jev-like "zero shot classifiers" or LLMs.

I feel like people in the field forgot everything.

LLMs, and other transformer models before them like BERT for example, have the benefit of "transfer learning."

If you want to make a ticket classification model, you don't need to train across many customers doing ticket classification, who might not want you to train on their data and whose data is impossible to obtain unless you already are a large company. Instead, you can train on a completely different task which forces the model to learn the syntactic and semantic structure of the English language — say predicting missing words in Wikipedia articles, which you can't do successfully without a good understanding of English — and then fine-tune that model on your specific task with much less data.

Because the initial task is so general, you can have one company do the expensive pretraining, share the base model, and then have everybody else just do the finetuning on their (small) proprietary dataset.

LLMs and models like Jev go one step further, letting you use them as classifiers with no training at all, with nothing but rules in the prompt. And with a few tricks, you can indeed use them to get pretty high-quality labels, which you can then distill into a fine-tuning dataset for a much smaller model.

children.author: abhgh
children.text:
Agree to all of this but I would make a minor correction: the interpretability is true under certain conditions, e.g., you use something like n-grams and train an SVM with a linear kernel. You could change the representation back then too, e.g., LDA (topic models), Latent Semantic Indexing, and of course, you could change the SVMs kernel as well, e.g., use a sequence kernel [1]. Some of these were much less interpretable. But the common pipeline back then was indeed n-grams + Linear SVM. Today it is easy to modernize the pipeline by just changing the representation step to use an embedder like ModernBERT. I have a "one page" classifier if you want to try it out - [2].

[1] I went down the rabbit hole of using sequence kernels quite a bit back then, see https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.13800, but the timing was terrible. RNNs and variants like LSTMs were beginning to become popular, and everyone (including me) switched.

[2] https://pocket-text-lab.abhishek-ghose-82.workers.dev/

Twice, I’ve asked it about a niche almost undocumented hardware register and it told me about fields that aren’t published anywhere…

True, but could be taken the wrong way. LLMs were also not able to train on that private customer data. They trained on so much general public data that they became capable enough to operate generally even on private data they had not been trained on.

That was the big breakthrough. I know that’s what you were trying to say, but on sites like this there are a lot of people who will see a comment like that and assume that LLMs like Sonnet were fed all of the private customer data that was withheld from training other models.

SVMs in big data were already well liked back in 2010 as they could be scaled via map-reduce.

An issue in industry was that companies would not allow training on their data across customers. Understandably so, as SVM dimensions are readily interpretable given some thought. General purpose datasets were ill-suited too depending on the task.

So you'd start from scratch every time, annotate features like crazy, and often didn't have enough training data overall.

LLMs "solved" that by just ignoring the previous rules and training on everything, which lets the necessary world knowledge seep back in.

I'm sure we'll see many combinations of LLMs and regular machine intelligence in the near future.

children.author: wat10000
children.text:
I see it as analogous to CPUs and specialized coprocessors. You don't want your general-purpose CPU bit-twiddling your USB data lines or decoding ethernet frames or blitting pixels. Specialized hardware does it so much more efficiently. And yet, powerful general-purpose CPUs remain common. Partly that's because there's a lot of complicated stuff being run that just isn't suited for specialized hardware; try making a C++ compiler coprocessor and see how far you get. And partly it's because that powerful general-purpose CPU is always present and can be instantly reconfigured to do anything. You'd rather use a dedicated cryptography coprocessor than implement your crypto on the CPU, but doing it on the CPU allows you to implement new crypto algorithms quickly. What's better: doing AES on a coprocessor on the CPU? Well, that depends on whether you have an AES coprocessor.

LLMs are the powerful general-purpose CPU of the ML world. Using an LLM as a classifier is woefully inefficient compared to using a dedicated classifier. On the other hand, that LLM exists right now and you can hook it up in ten seconds. You could ask: why use an LLM when a dedicated classifier would be so much more efficient? You could also ask: why build a dedicated classifier when a sufficiently capable LLM is available off the shelf? Neither one is the right answer every time.

I think this kind of change will pop up more often.

In software engineering, we learned a long time ago that giant monoliths are not the answer. You want smaller, but specialized units that work together. They perform better at their specific task, are more maintainable, you can just upgrade one part of the system without having to impact the others, ....

I don't know where the focus on building a single model that can do everything comes from.

children.text:
Indeed, I learned pretty quickly that maintaining the line between "underreported information" and "information overload" is an indefinite challenge that evolves over time as context changes.

But the human team is what understands the big-picture context and the way it changes over time, so it makes sense for them to manage the triggers for the "this may be important" tickets—for them to then ingest and discern whether it's important. Ultimately, ticketing software is just a tool designed to distribute context-stamped information to humans who then discern what to do with it.

So I think just like all other productivity software, it's only as good as the human system in place that drives its usage. That explains the bloat as well—it's not its own system, it's a big old suite of tools that are each available to be implemented into a human system if desired, or ignored if not.

That makes sense, but a part of me is wary of introducing noise at such a scale and drowning out whatever signal remains.

Also ticketing systems in my (very) limited experience tend to be bloated pieces of software, so that adds a fun dimension to it.

children.author: SoftTalker
dansalvato
children.text:
Right, I didn't mean using tickets as a generic event log—the assumption is that someone would have set up triggers because they actually have a reason to have the data on hand, and it's a low-friction way of getting what they need without worrying about implementing new tools or systems. In a good human system, the trigger would be disabled once that info is no longer useful. (And in a bad human system it would just stick around until nobody knows what it's for anymore, haha.)

We also had tickets that would trigger scripts upon generation, e.g. an auto-generated "low disk space" ticket would then trigger a basic "disk cleanup" script, and close itself if enough space was freed to clear the threshold. Yes, it's comical that the ticket would do that—but hell, it worked great. It ran agnostically across thousands of differently-configured machines. And whether or not it was a human who clicked the "disk cleanup" button shouldn't determine the usefulness of having that event logged in the ticket database.

Point is, the whole system was a veritable Swiss Army knife that didn't necessarily have to equate a "ticket" (database entry) to "requires human intervention", provided there was a good human system in place to leverage the tool in a way that was productive for them.

I've never seen a ticket system used as just a dumping ground for data in auto-closed tickets. Seems like there would be better solutions for that, particulary for data you want to find later (in my experience, the search capability of ticket systems varies from poor to "don't bother, you won't find what you're looking for")

Anything else, that needs a human to interpret or take action on, yes, ticket systems get extremely wide usage.

In my past experience in IT, the ticketing system basically doubled as an aggregated event log, and it was a legitimately good use case. The monitoring software we ran on our thousands of client workstations and servers was extremely powerful and could capture any conceivable metric to use as a trigger for auto-generating a ticket.

So, a lot of tickets generated would simply just be data reports with some info dumped in the ticket description, designed to be auto-closed but possibly useful later as an easily-accessible timestamped reference to some data.

Lots of other auto-generated tickets were "probably not an issue but it should pass over the eyes of someone knowledgable about this server/network" tickets. Like Windows Event Log error roundups, CPU usage spikes, or specific triggers that were set up in the aftermath of some catastrophe to help preemptively avoid a repeat incident.

Anyway, tickets are a great "first line of filtration" where you can take a massive ingest of all different kinds of data (hardware metrics, system logs, network activity), apply meaningful human context ("This pattern could be a sign of xyz"), and store it in a unified database. With that use case, it's easy to imagine a company with millions of customers and millions of servers producing millions of tickets.

No, serious question; there are no downvote controls on this "advertisement", what gives?

Founder of Seldon AI (www.seldon-ai.com) here. We are working on dev tools to help developers with this kind of refactoring and continual production work.

Basically there is a whole host of tarpit usage of LLMs in application backends today. This is simply another case of LLMs enabling people to build what they cannot productionize or maintain.

Today developers without any AI/ML skillset can prototype a fancy new feature with LLMs, what used to require collecting and curating data to train a pipeline of ML models then serving them in production.

The problem comes when it's time to take the new feature into production. That $20 cost with prototype/beta workload is now $30k per month in LLM costs, and those hallucinations that never happened on their 200 test samples is happening 600 times per day.

They are then stuck, because they lack the knowledge and budget to build and run the production ML pipeline properly, the infra stack necessary to handle production workload. Management also doesn't understand why they have to invest in rebuilding something that "seems to work" with "outdated methods".

These system one or decision models are a step up from LLMs when it comes to this usage. Problem is that they are still difficult to work with (limited in expression power) for many application logic. Despite the initial popularity, I hear about a lot of frictions refactoring LLM based backend with them, and multiple cases of production rollbacks to LLMs already.

I think system one models is a sensible paradigm, and we are on the precipice of something great, but there is a lot more work needed above the model layer to make this work.

Because LLMs (and many other ML systems) are chaotic, it is possible to manipulate them into doing something unexpected through a small, apparently innocuous change to their input. These changes can be illegible to human observers, which makes them harder to detect and prevent.

Ticket classification isn't necessarily so simple, and I can think of various reasons for using ML to classify tickets.

1. Some auto-generated ticket (e.g. a trigger from unusual hardware activity or a log entry) resembles a previous ticket that had meaningful action on it, addressed and solved by a specific team. That ticket could spend a week getting ignored or punted around when the right team can solve it in 5 minutes. ML could detect the similarity and reclassify it by that metric. 2. Human-submitted tickets are annoyingly fallible. For example, an "I can't log into my account" ticket could be auto-classified as "account recovery". Or maybe, e.g. the ticket system attaches a recent activity log from that IP address to be cross-checked by ML, which finds 5xx errors and reclassifies it for the technical team.

These are generic examples, but you can use your imagination and see how a company as huge as Amazon could benefit from this. I think it's for the purpose of minimizing the number of tickets that need to be manually reclassified because the wrong info was given to the wrong person.

children.text:
Zero-shot models like Jev or others can still be difficult to prompt tune. A lot of times you are describing how you want things to be classified (called label verbalization), and miss nuances about how the model does interpretation of that.

I have started working on models that can both do a classification without explanation, but enable a "think" mode that briefly explains its decision. So if you want to keep track of failures and figure out why the model doesn't like them, then you have a direction to try fixing it.

I'd like to try wrapping this in some kind of GEPA-like process to automate tuning based on your labeled examples using the supervision of a larger reflection model.

https://huggingface.co/dleemiller/AbsoluteZero-nli-4b

Decision models are much cheaper/faster to serve. For classification, you still need to do classic classification ML evaluation, but for many problem spaces you can get to ~90% of the power of a custom classifier model with an off the shelf decision model with just some prompt tuning.

One of the biggest issues with using a general LLM like Sonnet is calibration. I think Jev really helped bring this to light. With Sonnet, you get an answer and that's it. It's really not that great for classification, especially tagging.

I've trained a lot of NLI models, which do similar things to decision models. A 1B parameter encoder is about the same capability as a 2B LLM, but if you have multiple tags to check, it's not as efficient because you can't cache the bidirectional attention. On the other hand, they do seem to do a bit better on calibration.

I keep a leaderboard here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/dleemiller/open-nli-leaderboar...

children.author: zkmon
ActorNightly
children.text:
From a technical perspective, all of the previous ML work that happened before LLMs is basically encapsulated in LLMs.

For exmaple, SVMs are exactly neural nets in representation. Transformers are Kernel Machines in esssence - take your sequence of tokens across n dimentions, and thats your higher level space where you can make decisions on the output. Gradient boosting/decision trees are your backpropagation and RL, except on a latent space rather than direct data output.

And you don't really need to use all the old techniques anymore given the local inference that exists. For example,

https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/functiongemma

https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-...

Both of those run quite fast on CPU, and can be used as a replacement for a lot of traditional techniques. For example, set up a system where user query first gets compared against instruction documents using embeddings, pick the best matching document, feed that instruction + user query into function gemma, which then generates a sequence of tool calls with the right inputs. Then finetune the instructions and/or function gemma for your use case.

The case of companies using Opus tokens for all things is a classic case of having enough profit to not have to worry about hyper optimization.

LLM is a hammer that makes you see everything as an LLM usecase.

Recently people started equating all cognitive abilities to an LLM. Every foundational work that happened in ML and data science prior to LLm, are largely forgotten in the flood of LLM hype.

A lot of usecases would be far better off using some NLP or decision systems, or rule engines rather than paying for Opus. Big companies blindly use expensive frontier moels as a blanket solution irrespective of usecase fit, because they are chasing the goal of being an "AI-powered" company. LLM killed all othe simpler, specific solutions.
